explanation: Fires on subword pieces in the middle of rare technical words, mostly biomedical and scientific terms (arthro-pl-asty, aneur-ys-m, Staphy-loc-occus, s-elen-ite, Mycor-rh-iza), and also on fragments of math or code identifiers (arcc-os-ine, \to in limits, Unsafe in Swift pointer types). Ordinary whole words fire weakly or not at all.

Mixed bag. The strongest hits are the digit inside 'ISO-8859-1' and model/version-number digits; others include 'mal' in malice/malady/malonaldehyde, medical subword pieces, table separators, punctuation inside code and data, and some ordinary words. No single shared feature.

Fires on technical terms of art in specialist text: compiler flags and pragmas (-W, omp parallel, TRIGGER, !important), and scientific or engineering jargon pieces (Noetherian local, Reporter gene, racem-ates, voltam-metry, transist-ors, DNA meth-ylation). It is strongest when the token completes a fixed technical phrase. Everyday prose fires only weakly.

Fires on a subword piece in the middle of an uncommon multi-token word or name: tel-om-erase, \display-style, gyr-us, Clauser, frank-fur-ter, Wrig-ley, Yangt-ze, Sol-itaire. It also fires more weakly on member-access pieces in code (.create, .write, .com). It is strongest on the second fragment of a rare proper noun or technical word.

Fires on the token right after a style/attribute key in markup or code that sets visual properties such as color, border or stroke: the '="' after stroke-width or FontWeight, 'px' in '1px solid', the quote before a color name, ':' after border-style. Strongest in SVG/CSS/plot styling. Non-styling text gives almost nothing.

Fires inside postal addresses and affiliation lines, especially author-affiliation blocks in papers and the FSF address in license headers. Strongest on the first digit of a ZIP or postal code (MA 0|2139, D-|5311) and on institution words (Laboratoire, Université, Department). It fires more weakly on the first digit of years in copyright lines.

Fires on the first subword fragment of a word that has been split into several tokens, i.e. the piece right after a word boundary that starts a longer word (se-psis, Eins-ch-üchterungen, enf-antillages, un-tr-oubled, AUT-OC-OMMIT, g-annets, f-oment). It works across languages. Whole common words do not fire.

Fires in quantity, number and address formats, on the token that follows or continues a number: units after numbers (13 ounces, 20 seconds), the space before the next number in '14 feet, 8 inches' or '2 hours and 45', ZIP code digits and hyphens, citation page digits, and 'address' in 'shipping/mailing address'. It also fires on some unrelated code-import names (TypedArray, ZonedDateTime, random) and the CNN dateline.

Fires on words that describe spatial layering or relative position (on top, superimposing, sequentially deposited, lower half, behind, upon, underneath, over-lying) and also on parts of journal titles in citations (Neuroscience Methods, Neuropsychologia, J. Med. Chem, Cell Host Microbe). Two rough themes, and many top hits are loose.

Fires on the 'n' (or '=') of a sample-size annotation in parentheses in scientific abstracts, e.g. '(n = 20)' or '(N = 102)'. It is strongest right after '(' and requires a study/group context. It also fires on '=' in code attribute assignments (ou=, CommonName). Other uses of 'n' or 'normal' fire only weakly.

Fires on the second or later token of a multi-token proper name or identifier where the first piece predicts the rest: framework class/API names in code (AttributeSet, .onCreate, .Toast, HttpServletRequest, GeneratedValue, localhost after http://), plus named-entity continuations in prose (National End-owment, House Judiciary, Stephan-opoulos, CarG-urus). It is strongest in Android/.NET/Java code.

Fires mainly on code-syntax tokens in declarations: 'get'/'set' inside C# property braces { get; set; }, 'void' in type declarations, '=' in MATLAB assignments, "('" after require, and extern "C". A separate set of top hits is Arabic/Islamic names (Allāh, Allahu, Knesset).

Mixed bag: '{' in JavaScript destructuring const { ... } = require, 'v' in legal case captions (X v. Y), 'RE' in 'IN RE', fragments of rare proper names (Giar-utana, Butt-igieg, St-orch), the middle bytes of multibyte CJK/Greek characters, and some others. No unifying feature.

Fires on a non-first subword piece inside multi-token proper names of places, institutions and organizations, often non-English (Seoul National, China National Knowledge, Bharatiya Jan-ata, BE-IJ-ING, Tian-jin, Ben-Gur-ion, Tanger-ang, Zend Technologies). It also fires on path pieces such as linux/kernel. It is strongest when the token continues a named entity.
